# Souppaya, Scarfone and Dodson, Secure Software Development Framework v1.1

**Source:** Souppaya, Scarfone and Dodson (2022), *Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1*, NIST SP 800-218. DOI: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218. United States public domain; worldwide reprint and derivative-work permission under NIST Technical Series Publications policy. Republished courtesy of the National Institute of Standards and Technology.
**Structure:** Introduction; four groups of secure-development practices with tasks, notional examples and reference mappings; bibliography; EO 14028 mapping, acronyms and change-log appendices.

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The authors recommend integrating secure-development practices throughout an existing software development life cycle to reduce released vulnerabilities, mitigate exploitation of remaining vulnerabilities and prevent recurrence by addressing root causes. [AR] (Abstract, p. ii; §1, p. 1)

SSDF describes outcomes and a common vocabulary while leaving implementation to organisations, with choices tailored to risk, cost, feasibility, applicability and automatability. [AR] (§1, pp. 2–3)

## Interpretation and Audience

1. Producers of any size, sector or maturity and software acquirers are the main audiences; understanding the document requires no secure-development expertise, but implementing the recommended practices does. [AP] (Audience, pp. iii–iv)
2. Addressing security earlier generally reduces the eventual effort and cost required for the same security level, which the authors call shifting left. [AR] (§1, p. 1)
3. Practice order implies neither priority nor implementation sequence, and no notional example or combination of examples is required. [AP] (§2, p. 4)
4. Shared-responsibility arrangements should specify which provider or tenant owns each practice/task and how providers attest to conformance. [AP] (§1, p. 3)

## Prepare the Organization (PO)

5. PO.1 identifies and maintains security requirements for development infrastructure, processes and software, and communicates requirements to commercial-component suppliers. [AP] (Table 1, PO.1, pp. 5–6)
6. PO.2 defines responsibilities, supplies role-based training with proficiency review, and obtains leadership commitment; one example assigns a leader or leadership team accountability for the secure-development process and production release. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PO.2, pp. 6–7)
7. PO.3 specifies and securely maintains toolchains and generates evidence of performed practices, including assigning responsibility for evidence tools cannot produce. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PO.3, pp. 7–8)
8. PO.4 defines security-check criteria and gathers/protects supporting information; examples record approvals, rejections and exception requests and review criteria-based automated decisions. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PO.4, p. 8)
9. PO.5 separates and protects development environments and hardens development endpoints using risk-based practices. [AP] (Table 1, PO.5, pp. 8–9)

## Protect the Software (PS)

10. PS.1 protects all forms of code with least-privilege access, with examples including attributed version history, code-owner approval, signing and hashes. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PS.1, p. 9)
11. PS.2 makes release-integrity verification information available to acquirers, with examples using release hashes and code signing. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PS.2, p. 10)
12. PS.3 archives releases and supporting data and maintains/shares component provenance, for example through an SBOM updated when components change. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PS.3, p. 10)

## Produce Well-Secured Software (PW)

13. PW.1 designs against security requirements and risks, maintains decisions and exception rationales, and supports standard security services where appropriate. [AP] (Table 1, PW.1, p. 11)
14. PW.2 reviews design through qualified people uninvolved in its creation and/or automated toolchain processes to check requirements and risk information. [AP] (Table 1, PW.2, p. 12)
15. PW.4 reuses well-secured components when feasible and verifies third-party components against requirements throughout their life cycles. [AP] (Table 1, PW.4, pp. 12–13)
16. PW.5 applies coding practices appropriate to the language, environment and requirements; developer self-review is an example that complements other people or tools. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PW.5, p. 13)
17. PW.6 chooses security-capable compiler/interpreter/build tools and implements approved configurations. [AP] (Table 1, PW.6, p. 14)
18. PW.7 selects and performs code review/analysis and records and triages findings and recommended remediations. [AP] (Table 1, PW.7, pp. 14–15)
19. PW.8 selects, scopes, designs, performs and documents executable security testing, with examples including functional security tests, dynamic tests, regression tests and fuzzing. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, PW.8, p. 15)
20. PW.9 defines, implements and documents secure defaults that do not weaken security supplied by the surrounding platform, network or services. [AP] (Table 1, PW.9, p. 16)

## Respond to Vulnerabilities (RV)

21. RV.1 gathers and investigates credible vulnerability reports, continues code analysis/testing, and establishes disclosure/remediation policy with supporting roles and processes. [AP] (Table 1, RV.1, pp. 16–17)
22. RV.2 assesses vulnerability risk and implements prioritised responses; examples include temporary mitigation, risk acceptance/transference, advisories and trusted remediation delivery. [AP] [AE] (Table 1, RV.2, pp. 17–18)
23. RV.3 analyses root causes and recurring patterns, proactively removes similar vulnerabilities and updates the SDLC to reduce recurrence. [AP] (Table 1, RV.3, pp. 18–19)

## Key Statistics

| Fact | Value and source |
|---|---|
| Framework groups | Four: PO, PS, PW and RV. [AP] (§2, p. 4) |
| Position papers received in response to EO 14028 §4 alongside a June 2021 workshop | More than 150. [AP] (Acknowledgments, p. iii) |

## Key Connections

- The common-language approach is compared to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, while a footnote says SSDF practices do not map to CSF Functions/Categories/Subcategories and are typically different parties' responsibility. [BT] (§1, p. 2, footnote 2)
- Table 1 maps tasks to established guidance, including OWASP ASVS **4.0.3**, MASVS 1.4.2, SAMM 1.5 and SCVS 1.0 as listed in the 2022 bibliography. [BT] (References, pp. 20–23)
- Appendix A maps EO 14028 Section 4e subsections to SSDF practices/tasks using a risk-based approach; Appendices B and C supply selected acronyms and the final/draft change history. [AP] (Appendices A–C, pp. 24–27)

## Signature Contrarian Positions

The authors explicitly reject treating SSDF as a uniform checklist, prioritised sequence or mandatory set of implementation examples; risk and local context govern application. [AP] (§1, p. 3; §2, p. 4)
